pySASred: API reference

Generated from the docstrings.

Reduction of one run

Reduction of a single run to I(q):

read -> counting error -> dead time -> attenuator -> monitor (or time)

-> geometry and solid angle -> [detector efficiency] -> radial or sector average

Result: monitor-normalised intensity per steradian, I(q) in units of counts / monitor / sr, with the exact first-order propagation of every source. The detector efficiency comes from a water run (efficiency_from_runs()); transmission and background subtraction of the sample, thickness and absolute scale are phase 3.

pysasfit.sasred.reduce.efficiency_from_runs(water, empty_cell, beam_center_px, t_water, t_empty=None, mask=None, blocked=None, instrument=None, normalise_by='monitor', reject_sigma=5.0, water_k=None)[source]

Detector efficiency from water (see pysasfit.sasred.core.efficiency).

water, empty_cell, blocked: a raw run or a list of runs (summed) at the same detector distance and wavelength (empty_cell and blocked may be None); t_water, t_empty: transmissions as (value, sigma) or plain numbers; mask: the mask of the water data (default: the suggested mask of the summed water counts, border + beamstop + hot pixels). Every run is corrected for dead time and attenuator and normalised (monitor or time) as in reduce_run_1d(). reject_sigma: see efficiency_from_water() (beamstop edge). water_k: the angular dependence K(2θ)/K(0) of the water (a function of 2θ in rad, e.g. K() from water at two distances); the water image is divided by it so that the map holds the detector efficiency only.

Parameters:

  • instrument (dict | None)

  • normalise_by (str)

  • reject_sigma (float | None)

Return type:

Raw files (SANS-I, SANS-LLB)

Raw files of the SINQ SANS instruments: the reader is chosen from the file (SANS-I entry1/SANS, SANS-LLB entry0/SANS-LLB).

pysasfit.sasred.io.raw.instrument_of(path)[source]

“sans_i” or “sans_llb” (from the content of the file).

Return type:

str

SINQ SANS-LLB raw files (sans-llb<year>n<run>.hdf, NeXus entry0).

SANS-LLB has three detector banks:

  • central: 128 x 128 monoblock (5 mm pixels) on the detector carriage (central_detector);

  • left and bottom: wide-angle panels of 16 3He tubes (13.4 mm apart, 5 mm pixels along the tubes) on a second carriage closer to the sample (left_detector, bottom_detector). The direct beam never reaches them.

read_sans_llb() returns the run of the central detector as a RawRun (everything else in pySASred works on it unchanged: beam centre, masks, transmissions, catalogue, reduction table). The panels travel along in RawRun.panels; bank_run() turns one of them into a run of its own whose geometry comes from the pixel positions (panel_geometry()), so that the same reduction (dead time, attenuator, monitor, transmission, background, water, absolute scale per pixel, averaging) works on it.

Coordinates: NICOS writes, for every bank, the pixel positions posx/posy [mm] in one frame perpendicular to the beam (<bank>_data/posx|posy); the central detector has posx = 0, posy = 0 at pixel (63.5, 63.5) and posx decreases with the column. The beam position in that frame follows from the beam centre on the central detector (pixel indices). The positions of the panels as written are nominal: their offsets (dx, dy along posx, posy and dz along the beam, in mm) are calibration values, set under Settings → Preferences → pySASred → SANS-LLB wide-angle panels (or given to panel_geometry()).

Uncertainty engine

UArray: a value array that carries its exact first-order sensitivities to named, independent uncertainty sources.

Every quantity y in pySASred is represented as

y = value, dy = sum_s J_s ds, ds ~ (0, diag(var_s)), sources independent,

where s runs over named sources (the counts of a run, a monitor count, a transmission, a dead time, …). A source is a vector of n_s independent elements (n_s = 1 for a scalar such as a monitor count, n_s = number of pixels for the counts of a detector image).

For each source the Jacobian J_s (shape out x n_s, out = y.size) is stored in a structured form that stays small through every step of a SANS reduction:

J_s = S_s + U_s V_s^T

with S_s a scipy.sparse CSR matrix (diagonal for pixel-wise steps, banded or block-sparse after averaging) and U_s V_s^T a low-rank part (out x k, n_s x k). A scalar source is a low-rank term with V = [[1]]. The low-rank part arises when a pixel-wise quantity is multiplied by a function of an aggregate of the same counts (for example a dead-time factor that depends on the total count rate): it is the exact rank-1 coupling, never a dense N x N matrix.

Sensitivities to the same source add linearly, so a shared term (the Cd run in sample and empty cell, the same monitor in numerator and denominator) is never counted twice. Variances and covariances follow as

Cov(y) = sum_s J_s diag(var_s) J_s^T .

The propagation is exact to first order. The only approximation is the linearisation itself, which is validated against Monte Carlo in the tests.

Correction steps

Counting error of raw data (correction step 3).

Two exact models (doc: “Counting error of raw data”):

  • variance (default): sigma^2 = N, the exact variance of a Poisson count, the correct input for propagation and binning because variances add.

  • interval: the exact central 1-sigma Poisson confidence interval (Garwood), alpha = Phi(-1) per tail. Its half-width is for display and single-pixel use; it is not used for propagation.

pysasfit.sasred.core.counting.counts_uarray(counts, key, unit='counts')[source]

Raw counts as a UArray whose own elements are the independent Poisson source key with variance N.

Parameters:

  • key (str)

  • unit (str)

Return type:

UArray

pysasfit.sasred.core.counting.garwood_interval(counts, alpha=0.15865525393145707)[source]

Exact central Poisson confidence interval for observed counts N.

lower = P^{-1}(N, alpha) (0 for N = 0) upper = P^{-1}(N + 1, 1 - alpha) with P the regularised lower incomplete gamma function, which is the chi-square quantile form of Garwood (1936).

Returns (lower, upper, sigma) with sigma = (upper - lower) / 2.

Parameters:

alpha (float)

pysasfit.sasred.core.counting.ALPHA_1SIGMA = 0.15865525393145707

one-sided tail probability of a central 1-sigma interval, Phi(-1)

Dead-time correction (correction step 4), non-paralysable model.

N_true,i = N_i * f, f = 1 / (1 - tau * R), R = (sum of counts) / t

for a multiwire detector (one global rate). For tube detectors the rate is taken per tube (axis). The correction is applied to the UArray, so the exact sensitivity df/dN_j = f^2 tau / t of every pixel to every other pixel’s counts (a rank-1 coupling) and the sensitivity to tau are propagated.

pysasfit.sasred.core.deadtime.nonparalysable(counts, time_s, tau, axis=None, flag_limit=1.2)[source]

Return (corrected counts, factor, flag mask).

Arguments:

counts : UArray of raw counts (detector image, shape (ny, nx))

Pixel geometry (correction step 7) and solid angle (step 11).

Coordinates: pixel indices (iy, ix) are 0-based array indices of the stored image, axis 1 = columns (horizontal), axis 0 = rows (vertical), counted from 0 as in Python and GRASP (pixel centres at integers, pixel edges at half-integers).

Lab frame of pySASfit (docs/conventions.md, right-handed, as NXcanSAS/McStas): z along the beam (downstream), y vertical up, x horizontal = y × z, i.e. +x points to the LEFT as seen from the sample looking downstream and to the RIGHT in the views of pySASfit, which show the detector as seen looking towards the sample. The azimuth phi = atan2(y, x) is counter-clockwise in these views. The raw arrays of SANS-I and SANS-LLB have the column index growing to the right as seen from the sample, i.e. towards -x: column_sign = -1 (default).

The detector rotates about the vertical axis by alpha through the beam spot (the pixel position xc, yc where the undeflected beam hits it); SD is the distance from the sample to that spot along the beam. With s = column_sign:

u = (ix - xc) px,  v = (iy - yc) py                  (in-plane offsets along columns, rows)
r = (s u cos(alpha), v, SD + u sin(alpha))
n = (-s sin(alpha), 0, cos(alpha))                   (detector normal)

so that cos(psi) = n.r / |r| = SD cos(alpha) / |r| and the exact solid angle of a pixel of area A, to first order in A, is:

dOmega = A cos(psi) / |r|^2 = A SD cos(alpha) / |r|^3 ,

which reduces to A cos^3(2 theta) / SD^2 for alpha = 0.

Procedure (doc: “Beam centre and direct-beam profile”): exclude a rough mask (for example everything far from the beam), take the maximum pixel, then iterate the centre of gravity inside a disc of radius radius_px around the current estimate until it moves less than tol_px (default 0.1 pixel). pysasfit.sasred.core.averaging.q_edges(qmin, qmax, n, spacing='log')[source]

Direct-beam profile of a geometry: 2D Gaussian fit, beam divergence, and the geometric part of the q resolution.

The attenuated direct beam (beam stop out, no sample: the empty-beam transmission runs) shows on the detector what a point of the sample’s scattering pattern is smeared with by the collimation (source and sample apertures, their distance coll, the distance SD) and the detector’s own resolution. Its profile is fitted with a separable Gaussian integrated over every pixel plus a flat background,

N_ij = A [Phi((x_j + 1/2 - x0)/s_x) - Phi((x_j - 1/2 - x0)/s_x)]

[Phi((y_i + 1/2 - y0)/s_y) - Phi((y_i - 1/2 - y0)/s_y)] + B,

with Poisson weights on a window around the beam. Because the model is integrated over the pixel, s_x and s_y are the widths of the beam itself, without the pixel size (which the averaging accounts for separately). The angular widths seen from the sample are

sigma_theta_x = s_x p_x / SD, sigma_theta_y = s_y p_y / SD (rad, standard deviations),

and they give the geometric resolution of the scattering vector q = 2k sin(theta) (k = 2 pi/lambda): dq/d(2 theta) = k cos(theta), so in the direction phi on the detector

sigma_q,geo^2 = k^2 cos^2(theta) (sigma_theta_x^2 cos^2 phi + sigma_theta_y^2 sin^2 phi).

The second moments of the beam (as in the centre of gravity) are kept for comparison: a beam that is not Gaussian (box-shaped, with tails) shows as a difference between both widths.

pysasfit.sasred.core.beamprofile.collimation_profile(raw, instrument=None)[source]

Beam profile of the geometry of raw estimated from the collimation when no direct beam was measured: source aperture a1 (the neutron guide cross-section) at the distance coll before the sample aperture a2, detector at SD behind it. Each aperture adds a uniform distribution to the beam spot on the detector, a1·SD/coll (source projected through the sample aperture) and a2·(coll + SD)/coll (sample aperture seen from the source), so per axis

σ_spot² = (a1 SD/coll)²/12 + (a2 (coll + SD)/coll)²/12 , σθ = σ_spot / SD

(Mildner & Carpenter 1984, rectangular apertures). The apertures come from the instrument file (collimation.source_aperture_mm, collimation.sample_aperture_mm, (x, y)), replaced by the preferences (SANS reduction → Resolution: 50 × 50 and 8 × 14 mm² by default) for an instrument whose file has a collimation section (SANS-I; from_preferences: false there keeps the file values); coll and SD from the run. None when either is missing.

Return type:

BeamProfile | None

pysasfit.sasred.core.beamprofile.calibrated_profile(raw, profiles, instrument=None)[source]

Beam profile of the geometry of raw (no direct beam) from the collimation model calibrated on the measured direct-beam profiles of the same collimation length (profiles: {key: BeamProfile}; same wavelength preferred, else all wavelengths). The divergence is not simply copied: the sample-aperture term grows as 1/SD, so a shorter distance has a wider angular resolution. None when no direct beam of that collimation was measured (then collimation_profile()).

Return type:

BeamProfile | None

pysasfit.sasred.core.beamprofile.fit_apertures(measured, coll, a1_pref, a2_pref)[source]

Effective source and sample aperture widths (a₁, a₂) per axis [mm] from direct-beam profiles of one collimation length coll [m]: σ_spot² = (a₁² (SD/coll)² + a₂² ((coll+SD)/coll)²)/12.

Two or more detector distances: both widths, non-negative least squares on σ². One distance: the sample aperture of the preferences is kept and a₁ follows from the measured width (if the width is smaller than the sample-aperture term alone, a₁ of the preferences is kept and a₂ fitted instead). Returns ((a1x, a1y), (a2x, a2y), how).

Transmission from the beam behind a semi-transparent beam stop (SANS-LLB).

A semi-transparent beam stop lets a known, small fraction of the direct beam through. Its counts, in a transmission region of pixels drawn around the beam centre (the second layer of the mask editor: these pixels are used, not left out), measure the beam transmitted by the sample during the scattering run itself:

I_bs = sum over the region of the counts, corrected for dead time and attenuator, per monitor (or s) T_bs = I_bs(sample run) / I_bs(reference run)

with a reference run of the same configuration and beam stop: the empty beam, or the empty cell (then T_bs is the transmission of the sample relative to the cell). Scattered neutrons that land in the region are counted too, so T_bs is slightly too high for strong scatterers; how reliable it is, is what compare() shows against the transmission from the transmission runs (beam stop out).

The uncertainties come from the same propagation as the reduction (counting, monitor, dead time, attenuator; pysasfit.sasred.data.uarray): sigma statistical, sigma_total including the systematic sources that do not cancel in the ratio (e.g. different attenuators).

Which neutron monitors sit before and which after the velocity selector.

A monitor in front of the selector sees the white beam: its ratio to the proton beam (integrated_beam, the proton charge) does not change with the wavelength or the selector tilt. A monitor behind the selector sees what the selector passes, and its ratio changes with λ (source spectrum, selector transmission) and with the tilt (flux roughly ∝ dλ/λ). Only a monitor behind the selector cancels a change of the selector setting when the data are normalised by it.

selector_test() compares the ratio monitor / proton beam between groups of runs at different (λ, tilt). It needs runs at two or more settings; with one setting it says so.

For each setting the median of monitor/proton is taken (runs with proton charge and at least min_counts monitor counts, at least min_runs runs; a frame of a selector speed scan counts alone); the scatter within a setting (median relative deviation) is the noise. The monitor is before the selector when the medians of all settings agree within max(3·noise, 5 %), after the selector when they differ by more than max(5·noise, 15 %); in between, or with fewer than two settings, undetermined.

q resolution: one Gaussian sigma_q per point (1D) or a 2D Gaussian per pixel.

Three contributions, added in quadrature:

  • wavelength: sigma_q = q sigma_lambda/lambda, along q (the velocity selector’s triangular distribution: sigma = FWHM/sqrt 6);

  • geometry: the direct-beam profile of the geometry (pysasfit.sasred.core.beamprofile), angular widths sigma_theta_x, sigma_theta_y: in the direction phi on the detector sigma_q^2 = k^2 cos^2(theta) (sigma_theta_x^2 cos^2 phi + sigma_theta_y^2 sin^2 phi), k = 2 pi/lambda, dq/d(2theta) = k cos theta;

  • pixels: in 1D the spread of the pixel q inside each bin (which contains the pixel size); in 2D the pixel width, (k cos theta p/SD)^2/12 per detector axis.

Without a direct-beam measurement of the geometry the resolution is not determined (the reduction goes on without it and says so).

2D Gaussian resolution of every pixel: standard deviations along the detector axes (q_x, q_y) and along / across q (parallel = radial, perpendicular = azimuthal), and the q_x-q_y correlation.

Detector image in polar coordinates (azimuth φ, scattering vector q) for display.

φ = 0 is the horizontal direction +x of the lab frame (to the right in the view towards the sample; the raw columns run towards -x, column_sign = -1), increasing counter-clockwise (towards +y = up, axis 0), as the azimuth phi of pysasfit.sasred.core.geometry.pixel_geometry() (docs/conventions.md). Every cell of the (q, φ) grid takes the value of the detector pixel that contains its centre (nearest-pixel resampling, no interpolation: counts are not mixed); cells outside the detector are NaN. Pixel sizes may differ in x and y.

PolarImage

Detector efficiency (flood) from a water measurement.

Water scatters almost isotropically, so after the usual corrections its image is flat apart from the efficiency of the detector pixels:

I_water = [ (W - B) - (T_w / T_ec) (EC - B) ] / (T_w ΔΩ)

with W, EC and B the monitor-normalised images of water, empty cell and (optionally) the blocked beam, T_w and T_ec the transmissions and ΔΩ the solid angle of each pixel. The efficiency is this image divided by its mean over the valid (unmasked) pixels.

Masked pixels (behind the beamstop, hot pixels, …) have no water data. The SANS-I detector is a multiwire detector read out in coincidence: a pixel is the crossing of an x wire and a y wire, so its efficiency is approximately the product of a row and a column factor, ε(i, j) ≈ a_i · b_j. The masked pixels are therefore filled with

ε(i, j) = R_i · C_j / m,

R_i the mean efficiency of the valid pixels of row i (same y wire), C_j that of column j (same x wire) and m the mean of all valid pixels (1 by construction). A pixel whose whole row or whole column is masked (the standard border) has no estimate: its efficiency is set to 1 and it gets the mask bit EFFICIENCY.

Edge of the beamstop: pixels in the half shadow of the beamstop are not always in the mask of the water run, and their low “efficiency” would then be applied to the sample. Valid pixels within edge_px pixels of the masked area (not counting the border) whose value differs from the row x column estimate by more than reject_sigma statistical standard deviations are therefore rejected and filled like the masked ones (iterated until no new pixel is rejected). Elsewhere a deviating pixel is kept: it may be a real local defect.

The efficiency is a UArray: it keeps its exact sensitivities to the counts and monitors of the water and empty-cell runs and to the transmissions, so dividing a sample image by it propagates all of them (also the correlations it causes between the q points). Saved to a file (Efficiency.save()), only the standard deviation per pixel is kept; Efficiency.load() makes it one independent source per pixel (flood:<name>), which drops the (small) correlations between pixels.

Efficiency

Archive of detector-efficiency maps in one HDF5 file, to follow the detector over time.

Every archived map is one NeXus entry of the archive file, named after the date of its water measurement, e.g. /2026-10-02_SD-8.0m_6.00A_run82280 with efficiency (NXdata: the map, its errors, the filled / undefined / rejected pixels, the row and column profiles of the wires), instrument (the configuration of the water measurement: detector distance and tilt, pixel size, beam centre, wavelength and its spread, collimation length, attenuator) and process (runs, transmissions, comment, all metadata). The file attribute default points to the newest map, so viewers (pyTOOLbox) show it first. Summary numbers are kept as attributes of each entry, so the archive can be listed without reading the maps:

from pysasfit.sasred.efficiency_log import archive_efficiency, list_maps, load_map, history, plot_history
archive_efficiency(eff, comment="after HV change")   # archive file: Preferences, or path=...
list_maps()                     # one dict per map, oldest measurement first
load_map("2026-10-02_SD-8.0m_6.00A_run82280")        # an Efficiency (default: the newest)
history()                       # every map against the oldest one of its configuration (or reference=...)
plot_history().savefig("efficiency_history.png")

The archive file is Preferences → SANS reduction → efficiency archive file; empty means efficiency_archive.h5 next to the pySASfit preferences file. Command line:

python -m pysasfit.sasred.efficiency_log [archive.h5] [--plot history.png]

Reduction of table rows (2D, then average)

Reduction of a row of the reduction table: first the 2D image, pixel by pixel, then the radial (or sector) average.

Per pixel ij, every run corrected for dead time and attenuator and normalised to the monitor (or time), the runs of a row summed (reduce.combined_normalised_counts()):

N_ij = A · (S - Cd)/T_S - (1 - p_cS) · (SB - Cd)/T_SB (sample - background)

with water (Strunz et al. 2000, eq. 8; BerSANS SANSAniDo eq. 2):

W_ij = (W - Cd)/T_W - (WB - Cd)/T_WB dΣ/dΩ_ij = N_ij / W_ij · K0 (1 - τ_W) / (4π τ_W d_S) [1/cm/sr], τ_W = T_W / T_WB

The water has the same geometry, so solid angle and pixel efficiency cancel.

Where water takes too long (long distances, long wavelengths) the absolute scale comes from the direct beam of the same geometry (beam stop out, usually attenuated) and a detector efficiency map ε_ij (mean 1; usually from the water of a shorter distance, efficiency_from_runs()):

Φ = Σ_beam (DB - Cd)_kl / ε_kl [counts/monitor, attenuator corrected] dΣ/dΩ_ij = N_ij / (ε_ij ΔΩ_ij d_S Φ) · a_DB/a_S [1/cm/sr]

The absolute efficiency of the detector and its λ dependence cancel between Φ and N; only the relative pixel efficiency is taken from the map. The attenuator of the direct beam enters with its factor from the instrument file (its uncertainty is propagated when the file gives one).

Without water and direct beam the image is put on a relative scale per steradian and thickness:

I_ij = N_ij / (ΔΩ_ij · d_S [· η_ij]) [counts/monitor/sr/cm]

Missing measurements do not stop the reduction; each one is stated in the notes: no Cd → nothing subtracted, no sample background → no background subtracted, no water background → water not corrected for its cell, no transmission → T = 1, no thickness → d = 1 cm.

Selecting and grouping runs

Selecting runs and grouping them into samples, as BerSANS’ Select many samples:

  1. Select the runs to work on: a run range, optionally a pattern (alternately use n runs and skip m), and conditions on any header item: text equal or matching a regular expression (EXP-.*), a number in a range (1.99 ≤ SD ≤ 2.01).

  2. Group the selected runs by header items, each with a ± tolerance (sample name exactly, temperature ± 1 K, field ± 0.01 T, pressure, shear rate, …): every group becomes one sample row of the reduction table, its runs summed.

Header items are the named entries of grouping.FIELDS (wavelength in Å, distances in m, …), the run kind (scattering / transmission) and every scalar entry of the raw files, by its path (hdf:sample/temperature, values as stored, e.g. the wavelength in nm).

Reduction table

Time series of one sample: the runs of a sample row reduced one by one (or in small bins) instead of summed, each with its time.

A sample row of the reduction table becomes a series with RowSet.series = True. The runs ticked in the row (the first to the last run of the series, set in the row’s Time series… dialog) are sorted by their start time and grouped into points:

  • series_bin = N: N consecutive runs summed per point (1: every run is a point);

  • series_dt_s = Δt: all runs whose middle lies in the same time window of Δt seconds (instead of N).

The time of a point is the count-weighted middle of its runs, t = Σ M_i t_i / Σ M_i (M: monitor or measuring time, t_i = start + measuring time / 2), relative to t₀: series_t0 (date and time, e.g. the mixing or the temperature jump) or, when empty, the start of the first run of the series.

Every point is reduced with the corrections of its geometry exactly like a summed row; its results carry time_s (and time_start, time_end, series, series_t0, series_index), written into the output files and usable as a series key in pyTOOLbox.

Later: runs with many frames (time scans in one file) give the points in the same way (RawRun.frames).

pysasfit.sasred.series.SERIES_KEYS = ('time_s', 'time_start', 'time_end', 'series', 'series_t0', 'series_index', 'series_runs')

result parameters that describe the time of a series point (also put into the files’ metadata)

The correction matrix and the sample table of one configuration (as in BerSANS’ data-reduction window): which runs are summed for the blocked beam (Cd), the water, the water background (empty cell), the sample background, the direct beam and every sample, with transmissions, scaling (thickness), attenuation factor and scattering probability.

The absolute scale (ReductionTable.scale_method()) comes from the water of this geometry or, where water takes too long (long distances, long wavelengths), from the direct beam of this geometry (attenuated, beam stop out) together with a detector efficiency map (usually made from the water of a shorter distance; ReductionTable.efficiency).

The table can be filled automatically from a Plan (runs grouped by metadata, outliers left out with the reason in the comment of the run) and edited or filled completely by hand. It is saved as JSON next to the reduced data.

pysasfit.sasred.reduction_table.from_plan(plan, config, raws=None, transmissions=None, sample_background='empty_cell')[source]

Fill the table of one configuration from a plan.

raws: run -> raw run (thickness, sample position); transmissions: rows of trans.txt (read_transmission_summary()), matched by sample name and, with raws, by sample position (a value measured at another changer position is not used; transmission runs at another position neither). Without a usable trans.txt value the transmission is computed from the transmission runs at the same position against the nearest empty-beam transmission run (beam spot τ); a trans.txt value that disagrees with the runs is flagged. A sample whose position is that of another sample (within 5 mm) is flagged (“changer not moved or wrong sample name?”), as is a sample measured at several positions; sample_background: the role whose runs fill Sample-BG when the plan has no sample background of its own (default: the empty cell, as when the samples sit in the same cells as the water; None leaves it empty).

Configurations with scattering runs, in the order of the plan.

Reduction plan

The reduction plan: which runs play which role, which were summed and which were left out.

For every instrument configuration (detector distance, wavelength, collimation) the runs are grouped by sample name and kind (scattering or transmission = direct beam with the beam stop moved out, usually attenuated), each group gets a role

  • sample: S (any other name);

  • sample_background: EB / SB, container or substrate of the sample (assign explicitly);

  • water: H2O for the efficiency and the absolute scale, W (H2O, water);

  • empty_cell: EC / WB, the empty water cell (EC, empty cell);

  • empty_beam: EH, open beam, transmission reference (EB, empty beam, open beam);

  • blocked_beam: Cd, blocked beam / electronic background (Cd, B4C, blocked);

and its repeated runs are checked before summing: scattering runs with grouping.check_runs() (when a beam centre and q bins are given), transmission runs by their count rate per monitor. Plan.markdown() gives the table to read, Plan.save() writes it as JSON next to the reduced data, so it can always be checked later which files were summed and which were outliers.

EB means empty beam at SANS-I (trans.txt gives it T = 1); the sample background (empty container of the samples) must be assigned explicitly with roles={"EC": "sample_background"} when the samples sit in the same cells as the water.

Scattering groups are checked with grouping.check_runs() when beam_center_px and edges are given (beam_center_px may be a function of the first raw run of a group, to use the centre of its geometry; mask may then take (raw, centre)); transmission groups by their count rate with rate_floor (0.5 %) for the beam stability (edges and mask may be functions of the first raw run of a group, e.g. to depend on SD).

Repeated transmission (direct-beam) runs: total counts per monitor with Poisson errors. Returns (verdict, outlier run numbers, χ²/ndf), with details also {run: (relative deviation from the mean of the kept runs, deviation in σ)}.

Parameters:

  • alpha (float)

  • monitor (str)

  • rel_floor (float)

  • details (bool)

Detector model

Physical model of the SANS-I ³He detector: transmission of the entrance layers and absorption probability in the detection gas, as a function of wavelength λ and of the angle ψ between the neutron path and the detector normal.

Layers (instrument file detector.construction): Al dome window (7 mm, Ø 1300 mm, radius of curvature 930 mm), pure ⁴He cover gas at 2.7 bar, a flat 2 mm Al membrane, then the detection gas at the same total pressure, 2.7 bar: ³He with CF₄ as stopping gas. The CF₄ partial pressure is not known; a conventional mixture (about 0.7 bar CF₄, ³He 2.0 bar) is assumed. Values still unknown (active depth, ⁴He path, the CF₄ fraction) are parameters (pressure_bar is the ³He partial pressure).

Cross sections (thermal, 1.798 Å; absorption ∝ λ):

  • ³He: σ_a = 5333 b;

  • Al: σ_a = 0.231 b, σ_inc = 0.0082 b; coherent (Bragg) scattering only below the cut-off λ = 2 d_111 = 4.68 Å; above it a small inelastic (phonon) part, taken as al_inelastic_b;

  • ⁴He: σ_s = 1.34 b, no absorption.

The mean conversion depth below the start of the active volume, ⟨z⟩, is where the neutron is detected on average: it is part of the effective sample-detector distance and shifts with λ.

pysasfit.sasred.core.detector_model.efficiency(wavelength_A, psi_rad=0.0, depth_m=0.03, window_m=0.007, membrane_m=0.002, membrane_al=True, pressure_bar=2.7, he4_bar=2.7, he4_path_m=0.0, al_inelastic_b=0.1)[source]

Detection probability: transmission of window, ⁴He and membrane times absorption in ³He. Relative to ψ = 0 this is the angular efficiency that water normalisation removes.

Parameters:

membrane_al (bool)

Water at two distances

Water measured at two detector distances.

A sample normalised by water measured at the same distance needs no solid-angle correction (it cancels pixel by pixel), but it inherits the angular dependence K(λ0, 2θ) of the water scattering, which in a flat cell is mostly multiple incoherent scattering (Strunz et al., J. Appl. Cryst. 33 (2000) 829, section 7 and fig. 4: more scattering along the cell normal).

The same pixel ij sees 2θ_a at distance L_a and 2θ_b at L_b. After the solid-angle correction the ratio of the two water images is free of the pixel efficiency η_ij:

I_a(ij) / I_b(ij) = C · K(2θ_a,ij) / K(2θ_b,ij)

so a fit of ln(I_a/I_b) = c + Σ_k a_k [(2θ_a)^{2k} - (2θ_b)^{2k}] gives K(2θ)/K(0) = exp(Σ a_k (2θ)^{2k}) and the constant c = ln C. In principle C = 1. A constant different from 1 means something that does not depend on the angle differs between the two distances, e.g.

  • an effective distance offset δ common to both (reference point of the distance, conversion depth in the detector): ΔΩ ∝ 1/(L + δ)² gives C = [(L_b + δ)/L_b]² / [(L_a + δ)/L_a]²;

  • a dead-time correction that is too small at the higher count rate (shorter distance);

  • a primary beam that is not the same per monitor count (collimation, attenuator, monitor drift).

The two first can be told apart by a third distance or by the same distance at another count rate (attenuator in).

Scattering strength

How strongly does a sample scatter? Transmission modes, the coherent scattering probability p_cS and the regime of the reduction formula (Strunz, Šaroun, Keiderling, Wiedenmann & Przenioslo, J. Appl. Cryst. 33 (2000) 829).

Symbols of the paper:

  • t_S transmission for absorption and large-angle coherent (Bragg) scattering;

  • T_Si = t_S (1 - p_iS): absorption and incoherent scattering (what a transmission measured over a wide solid angle gives once all small-angle scattering is collected: the plateau);

  • τ_S = T_Si (1 - p_cS): total removal transmission (what a transmission through the direct beam spot only would give; measurable only as an upper limit τ_UL > τ_S because neutrons scattered into the beam spot are always counted);

  • p_cS = d_S ∫ dΣ/dΩ dΩ: probability of at least one coherent small-angle scattering event.

The cross-section from a sample in a container or on a substrate (EB) is (their eq. 3/8)

[(S - Cd)/(T_EB T_Si) - (EB - Cd)/T_EB · (1 - p_cS)] / (d_S I_prim η ΔΩ)

so (1 - p_cS) multiplies the background, and T_Si (not τ_S) divides the sample. With τ_S in the first term (their eq. 9, aqueous samples where incoherent attenuation dominates) the whole curve is shifted by (1 - p_cS). BerSANS implements the general form with a user-given “scattering probability” p(S) (default 0) and a transmission whose meaning depends on the detector area used.

This module provides

  • aperture_transmission(): T(α) from a direct-beam run with and without sample, summed over growing discs; the plateau gives T_Si, the beam spot τ_UL, and 1 - τ_UL/T_Si ≤ p_cS;

  • scattering_probability(): p_cS from a cross-section in absolute units, with Guinier and Porod extrapolations outside the measured q range;

  • scale_probability() / thickness_for(): p_cS ∝ d λ² for single scattering;

  • assess(): the regime (weak / moderate / strong) and what to do;

  • self_consistent_probability(): the formula is an integral equation in p_cS; iterate reduce -> p_cS -> reduce until p_cS is stable.

pysasfit.sasred.core.scattering_strength.aperture_transmission(sample, empty, centre, pixel_size_m, SD_m, sample_var=None, empty_var=None, cd=None, cd_var=None, valid=None, radii_px=None, beam_fraction=0.99, flat_background='auto', n_rings=12)[source]

T(α) = Σ_disc(S - B) / Σ_disc(E - B) for discs of growing radius around centre, and the radially averaged sample/empty ratio per ring.

sample, empty (and cd) are images normalised to the same monitor (direct beam with and without the sample, beam stop out, attenuated as needed); the variances default to the values themselves (Poisson counts). pixel_size_m is (x, y) or one number.

Background B: the Cd run when given. Without one, flat_background="auto" takes the mean of the empty-beam run in the outer half of the detector as a flat, beam-independent background per pixel (a number can be given instead; None = no background). Without it, the large discs collect background in both runs and T(α) drifts towards 1 by about (1 - T) · B_total / E_total.

Grouping and equivalence of runs

Runs of one sample under the same conditions: grouping by metadata, then a check whether the runs of a group are statistically equivalent before they are summed.

Grouping follows BerSANS: a run belongs to a group when every selected metadata entry agrees within its precision (sample name exactly, temperature within ±0.5 K, SD within 1 %, …).

BerSANS then sums all files of the group. check_runs() adds what is missing there: it compares the reduced I(q) of the runs with their propagated uncertainties and tells

  • equivalent – the runs scatter as their counting statistics allow; summing is safe;

  • outlier – one or a few runs differ, the others agree (bubble, wrong position, beam trip);

  • scale drift / scale change – the runs differ by a q-independent factor only (fewer particles in the beam: sedimentation or creaming of the whole sample, a changed thickness or transmission, a normalisation problem); drift when the factor follows the measuring time;

  • shape drift / shape change – the curve itself changes (aggregation, size-selective sedimentation, a structural change); drift when a q band follows the measuring time.

Statistics (runs k = 1..n, q bins i, statistical uncertainties s_ki, weights w = 1/s²):

  • global χ² of all runs against the weighted mean, n_q (n-1) degrees of freedom;

  • leave-one-out χ²_k of run k against the mean of the others, with the covariance of both (the full statistical covariance of each run when it is given);

  • scale model I_ki = a_k μ_i: χ² with n_q (n-1) - (n-1) degrees of freedom and the factors a_k;

  • trends: weighted straight line versus the mid time of each run, for the scale factors and for the mean intensity in n_bands q bands (low q first), reported as relative change per hour and as z = slope / σ(slope).

An optional relative floor (rel_floor, added in quadrature to every point) accepts known instabilities below the counting statistics, e.g. 0.3 % beam or monitor drift.

Polarised data (SANSPOL)

SANSPOL: correction of half-polarised data (polariser and flipper before the sample, no spin analysis).

Measured states, one reduced data set each (2D image or 1D curve, fully corrected: background, cell, transmission, efficiency and absolute scale applied to every state as for unpolarised data):

polariser out -> I_u = (I+ + I-)/2 polariser in, flipper off -> I_off = n+_off I+ + n-_off I- polariser in, flipper on -> I_on = n+_on I+ + n-_on I-

I+ and I- are the cross sections for a fully polarised incident beam with the neutron spin parallel (+) and antiparallel (-) to the field at the sample, summed over the final spin states: I± = I±± + I±∓. With P the beam polarisation, f the flipped fraction of the flipper (flipper “efficiency” F = 2f - 1) and r the depolarisation factor of the sample:

Pe = P r, r = (1 - P_f) / (-ln P_f) (Quan et al., IUCrJ 8 (2021) 455; r = 1 for P_f = 1) n+_off = (1 + Pe)/2, n-_off = (1 - Pe)/2 n-_on = f n+_off + (1 - f) n-_off, n+_on = 1 - n-_on (exact) n-_on = f n+_off, n+_on = 1 - n-_on (“bersans”: Keiderling et al.,

Meas. Sci. Technol. 19 (2008) 034009, eq. 3b)

flipper_off_is_plus = False exchanges the roles of + and -. P_f is the polarisation measured after the sample in transmission (needs an analyser); without it, P_f = 1.

Inversion (two of the three states):

I+ - I- = (I_off - I_on) / (f Pe) (exact form) I_u = I_off - (I_off - I_on) / (2 f) (independent of P) I± = I_u ± (I+ - I-)/2

With all three states the two unknowns follow per pixel from weighted least squares (weights from the statistical variance), and chi² per pixel (one degree of freedom) checks the consistency of P, f and the scale of the polariser-out data. Without an analyser P and the magnetic contrast are degenerate: only P (I+ - I-) is measured, so P must come from the metadata, from the instrument table (SANS-I: Aswal et al., NIM A 586 (2008) 86) or from a separate measurement. f is the only efficiency that can be determined from the data (flipped_fraction_from_data(), needs all three states on the same absolute scale).

The correction is linear and is applied to the fully corrected data, never to raw counts (Keiderling et al. 2008). Uncertainties: the input UArrays keep all their sources (sources shared by the states, e.g. the same background or water, are counted once); P, f and P_f enter as systematic scalar sources (group polarisation) when their uncertainty is known, otherwise they are not propagated and a note says so.

Labels: + / - mean the neutron spin parallel / antiparallel to the field (Moon, Riste & Koehler, Phys. Rev. 181, 920 (1969)); then I+ - I- = +4 N·M for nuclear and magnetic amplitudes of the same sign. Michels, SASfit and part of the magnetic-SANS literature label by the neutron moment (antiparallel to the spin): there “++” is our “–” (Quan et al., J. Phys. Conf. Ser. 1316 (2019) 012010).

Masks

Detector masks: reason bits, the standard border, a suggested beamstop and hot-pixel mask from the data, pixel selection by shapes, and mask files.

A mask is a uint32 array of the detector shape; 0 = pixel used, any set bit = excluded, the bit says why:

bit

name

meaning

1

border

the standard mask: outer rows and columns of the detector

2

beamstop

beamstop shadow (suggested from the data, or the disc on the panel)

4

user

drawn or loaded by the user

8

deadtime

dead-time factor above the flag limit (set by the reduction)

16

hot

isolated pixels far above their neighbourhood (suggested)

32

efficiency

no detector-efficiency estimate (whole row or column masked in the water run)

Mask files (save_mask() / load_mask()):

  • .h5: NeXus-like HDF5, /entry/instrument/detector/pixel_mask (uint32, these bits, the bit names as attribute) with the beam centre, run and date; the default

  • .npy: the uint32 array

  • .txt: 0/1 matrix (1 = masked; loaded as user), e.g. for other programs

pysasfit.sasred.core.mask.suggest_beamstop(counts, beam_center_px, valid=None, search_radius_px=20.0, drop=0.3, smooth=3, grow_px=1, shape='rectangle')[source]

Beamstop shadow: the region around the beam centre where the intensity drops suddenly.

The image is median-filtered (smooth pixels) against counting noise. The rim level is the 90th percentile within search_radius_px of the beam centre (the bright scattering around the beamstop); every pixel below drop × rim level is “low”. The shadow is the connected region of low pixels that reaches to within 3 pixels of the beam centre, with holes filled and grown by grow_px pixels (the penumbra). With shape “rectangle” (default; the SANS-I beamstops are square) the whole bounding rectangle of that region is returned, with “shadow” the region itself.

Returns (bool mask, info dict); the mask is empty with info["reason"] when there is no shadow at the beam centre (e.g. a direct-beam run without beamstop).

Parameters:

  • valid (ndarray | None)

  • search_radius_px (float)

  • drop (float)

Files and units

SinqNexusSource: read SANS-I raw HDF5 files (correction step 1).

Missing required header fields raise an error; they are never replaced by defaults silently. Optional fields (absent in older files, e.g. the sample thickness before 2025) are returned as None and listed in missing_optional. Units are taken from the units attributes and converted: wavelength to Angstrom, distances to m.

exception pysasfit.sasred.io.sinq.MissingField[source]

Bases: KeyError

NXcanSAS 1D output with full uncertainty information.

Standard fields: I with @uncertainties = “Idev” (statistical part only), Q with @resolutions = “Qdev” (left out when the resolution was not determined: no direct-beam measurement of the geometry). 2D: Qx, Qy with @resolutions = “Qxdev” / “Qydev” (per pixel). Non-standard additions, all inside SASdata:

I_covariance_statistical   (n x n)  covariance of the non-systematic sources
I_systematic/<source>      sensitivity dI/ds of each systematic source,
                           with @sigma, @group (fully correlated scale terms)
I_budget/<source>          variance contribution of every source

Provenance goes to SASprocess: software, version, raw file paths and SHA-256, parameters and notes (for example “uncertainty unknown, not propagated”), and metadata: the header items of the raw run as JSON (metadata), used to group curves later.

pysasfit.sasred.io.nxcansas.write_nxcansas_1d(path, reduced, title=None, i_unit='arbitrary', units='nm')[source]

units: “nm” (Q in 1/nm, default) or “A” (Q in 1/angstrom).

pysasfit.sasred.io.nxcansas.write_nxcansas_2d(path, reduced, title=None, units='nm')[source]

The 2D image of a reduction (ReducedRun or Reduced2D) as NXcanSAS: SASdata with I (ny, nx), Idev (statistical), Qx, Qy (ny, nx; I_axes = “Qy,Qx”), Mask (1 = not valid) and the uint32 reason bits of pySASred (mask_bits); SASinstrument/SASdetector with distance, beam centre (pixels) and pixel size so that q and the azimuth can be recomputed; SASprocess as in 1D with the header items (metadata).

Plain-text output: q, I, Idev (statistical), Qdev, and the systematic standard deviation as a fifth column. The header lists the run, parameters and notes. Without a resolution (no direct-beam measurement of the geometry) Qdev is written as 0, as readers take a fourth column as the resolution, and the header says so.

pysasfit.sasred.io.ascii.write_ascii_1d(path, reduced, units='nm')[source]

units: “nm” (q, Qdev in 1/nm, default) or “A” (1/Å).

Transmission tables written during the beam time (trans.txt):

Summary of results:
-------------------
   Data file,    Sample name, Transmission, +/- Error
D0082267.001,            H2O,       0.2399,    0.0008

The data file names the transmission run (D0082267.001 = run 82267); the sample name links it to the scattering runs of the same sample, which have their own run numbers.

Bases: object

Where the beam stop is relative to the beam centre, per configuration (SD, λ).

The beam stop motors (bsx, bsy) [mm] are tied to detector pixels by the shadow of the beam stop in the scattering runs (ref_mm <-> shadow_px, signs sign from the instrument file); the beam centre comes from the direct-beam runs of the configuration (or of the same wavelength at another distance, or the shadow itself as the last resort). The distance of the beam stop from the beam centre on the detector then decides whether it is out of the beam.

pysasfit.sasred.catalogue.beam_centres(raws, borrow=True)[source]

Beam centre per geometry (SD, λ, coll) from its direct-beam runs (beam stop out): median of the masked centres of gravity, σ from their spread (or the statistical σ for one run). The solid angle and q of every pixel depend on it, so each geometry needs its own centre (gravity shifts it with SD and λ, the collimation coll changes the beam). With borrow a geometry without direct-beam run gets the centre of the same wavelength, preferably the same collimation, at the nearest distance, marked as borrowed.

GUI

pySASred Qt tool: SANS-I raw data to I(q) with full error propagation.

pysasfit-sasred [raw-data folder] python -m pysasfit.sasred.gui [raw-data folder]

Also hosted as the “pySASred” tab of the pySASfit launcher (the first tab).

Panels (every one detachable, View menu):

Runs           raw-data folder and the header table of its runs
Reduction      beam centre (from a direct-beam run or by hand), first-guess beamstop,
               q bins, units (nm or Å), normalisation, sector, live I(q);
               reduce the selected runs; save
Detector       2D image of the selected run (colour scale, cartesian or polar view)
               with beam centre and mask; mask tools (suggest, draw, undo, load, save)
I(q)           reduced curves with the statistical error bars (Idev) and the
               live radial average of the selected run
Error budget   relative standard deviation of each source versus q
Log            notes of every reduction (e.g. "uncertainty unknown, not propagated")

Numbers that are not on the panels (beam-centre disc radius and tolerance, start values of the panel fields) are in Settings → Preferences → SANS reduction.

pysasfit.sasred.gui.main(argv=None)[source]

Interactive mask editing in the detector panel of pySASred.

Tool bar below the colour-scale row of the detector plot:

  • Suggest – the mask for the image shown: standard border (2 outer rows and columns), beamstop shadow (sudden drop around the beam centre) and hot pixels (pysasfit.sasred.core.mask.suggest_mask()). Pixels you drew yourself are kept.

  • Tool – navigate (zoom / pan with the plot tool bar), or add (+) / remove (−) pixels with a rectangle, an ellipse, a polygon (click the corners, close it on the first one) or a brush (drag; size in pixels). Remove clears every reason of a pixel.

  • Undo / Redo (Ctrl+Z / Ctrl+Y), Reset (border only), Load… / Save… (.h5 with the reason bits, .npy, or a 0/1 .txt matrix), show (overlay).

  • edit – which of the two layers the tools draw on: the mask (pixels left out of the scattering) or the transmission region (pixels used, not left out: the direct beam behind a semi-transparent beam stop, whose counts give the transmission; see pysasfit.sasred.core.beamstop_transmission). The region is kept per instrument configuration like the mask and drawn as a green outline; Suggest proposes it around the beam centre.

Editing works in the cartesian view; the polar view shows the masked pixels in grey. The mask is used at once by the live I(q), the reduction and the polar view, and is kept with the last session.
